case_study.title: Discovery & Prototyping Hub
case_study.subtitle: From Figma to live code: a prototyping platform bridging design, AI, and development to validate experiences before writing production code.

problem.title: The Problem
problem.p1: In complex digital products — especially in HealthTech, where a web platform for operators coexists with mobile apps for professionals, patients, and drivers — the classic design flow creates critical frictions:
problem.li1: Static prototypes do not reflect real complexity. A Figma mockup cannot simulate loading states, real-time validations, or multi-step flows with dynamic data.
problem.li2: Handoff is a bottleneck. Developers receive PDFs or Figma links that do not match the real frontend component architecture.
problem.li3: Documentation becomes outdated at the first change. Specifications written in parallel to the prototype are rewritten with each iteration.
problem.li4: UX testing is expensive and slow. Coordinating sessions with real users for each iteration is unsustainable in agile cycles.

ai_usage.title: AI Agent Spend Control
ai_usage.subtitle: The request was to monetize the AI agents. The contracts didn't allow adding charges. I designed the system to measure and cut their spend instead, so the agents could launch without financial risk.
ai_usage.role_val: Product Designer, with a Business Analyst

cover.alt: Clinic balance panel: available and consumed credits, pockets sorted by expiry and consumption rules

problem.title: The Problem
problem.intro: The platform was about to launch AI agents (clinical notes, medical records, image analysis, support) that consume tokens from third-party models. That usage is a real variable cost, and nobody could see it:
items: The clinic (the customer) didn't know how much its team spent on AI agents and couldn't set limits.
The internal team had nowhere to run the resale: enabling packages, knowing what to invoice at month end, or measuring margin.
Every new agent added uncontrolled financial exposure for both sides.

insight.title: The pivot: measure in order to cut
insight.body: Existing contracts didn't allow adding charges to the invoice. Instead of designing screens for a pricing model that couldn't be applied, we reframed the scope: the MVP doesn't bill, it measures. The lever becomes a per-organization cut-off that stops agent usage without touching balance or settings. That's why "AI Billing" was renamed "AI Management".

flow.title: Two users, one loop
flow.desc: The clinic admin starts the flow and the internal team running the resale closes it.

steps.text: Sees the balance as two numbers (available and consumed) and credit pockets sorted by expiry, with the balance rules explained on the same screen.
Analyzes usage by agent and by user over a chosen period, and sets per-user limits so no one drains the team's balance.
When running low, requests a package. While it's pending, another one can't be requested.
Works a request queue sorted by decision urgency. Approving credits the balance instantly and logs who did it; rejecting requires a reason.
Sees which organizations consume most and on which agents, opens each one's profile and, if it hasn't paid, cuts off agent usage.
Closes the month in bulk: reads the broken-down resale margin and moves every approval to invoiced at once.

gallery.title: Prototype screens
gallery.desc: Screenshots and recordings of the working prototype with fictional data. The same baseline handed off to engineering (UI in Spanish).

items.caption: Usage over the period, with switchable grouping by balance source or by agent.
Internal ops: a request from a clinic with no balance is enabled from the queue. The balance is credited instantly and the log records who did it.
The per-organization cutoff: suspending the service requires a reason and keeps the clinic's balance and settings.
Month close: invoiced amount and margin per month, with margin shown as magnitude, not alarm.

decisions.title: Key decisions
decisions.desc: 76 decisions logged in about three weeks. These are the ones that shaped the product most.

items.title: Balance is consumed by expiry
items.body: What expires first is spent first, whichever pocket it comes from. A review caught that the order was reversed in the doc, the data and the UI; we fixed it the same day, in the prototype.

items.title: The screen explains its own rules
items.body: A balance with expiry dates is opaque. The explanation lives where the question comes up, not in a manual.

items.title: Margin is shown broken down
items.body: Resale margin is separated from the cost of the contractual quota, so the included quota never reads as a loss. A business decision before a visual one.

items.title: Magnitude, not alarm
items.body: Margin uses an ordinal color ramp instead of green and red: it conveys how much without implying something is wrong, and it's more accessible.

items.title: Low balance is flagged before zero
items.body: "Out of balance" is defined by a threshold, to warn before a clinician loses a tool mid-consultation.

items.title: The queue is sorted by urgency
items.body: Requests come first by how urgent the decision is, not by arrival date, and flag the organization that has already run out.

pivots.title: Course corrections
pivots.desc: 8 decisions were fully or partly reversed. It happened in the prototype, not in production, and the log records what replaced what.

items.before: Replicate a cloud provider's billing console, as a stakeholder asked
items.after: Users choose the analysis period, and that period never changes the balance
items.why: Instead of copying the screen, I researched what problem each control solved. That console separates when usage happened from which invoice it lands on: our exact problem, since packages expire after 30 days and quotas renew on each customer's anniversary.
A limit that doesn't limit isn't a limit, it's a warning, and it confused admins. Protecting a clinician mid-consultation is solved with advance warnings, not a second kind of limit.

items.before: All balance expires at calendar month end
items.after: Each package expires 30 days after approval
items.why: A package bought on the 10th can't expire on the 31st: it charged for a month and sometimes delivered six days. Fine print like that turns into complaints in production.

results.title: Validation and outcome
results.desc: The prototype was validated against seeded data, with a synthetic user and with the team, before reaching engineering.
items: It's now in production: the platform can launch AI agents with their spend measured and a per-organization cut-off available.

A full re-run of the validation guide found 4 bugs, fixed the same day. The main one: the per-user limit used the analysis period instead of the billing cycle, showing users as blocked when they weren't.
A synthetic user with an auditor profile walked the discovery: dense numbers read clearly, and one medium-severity finding surfaced (KPI cards were clickable but didn't look it).

items.title: Sometimes the best design move is changing the question.
items.body: "How do we monetize the AI agents?" had no viable answer. "How do we control their spend?" did, and it unblocked the launch.

items.title: Copying a screen isn't copying a solution.
items.body: A reference's value is in the problem each control solves, not in its layout.

items.title: Cheap reversals are an advantage.
items.body: With every decision logged, changing our minds cost a log entry, not a sprint.

summary.problem: The platform was about to launch AI agents with a variable cost nobody could see, and contracts did not allow passing it on to customers.
summary.solution: Reframe the scope: meter spend per organization, user and agent, with a per-organization cutoff as the lever.
summary.impact: In production: AI agents launch with metered spend and a per-organization cutoff available.

routes.title: Home-Visit Route Optimizer
routes.subtitle: A scheduling optimizer for home medical visits, where the system plans the week and the coordinator stays in control.
routes.role_val: Product Designer, with a Business Analyst

cover.alt: Day schedule as a Gantt per clinician, already optimized, with kilometers and appointments metrics and the missed-visits panel

problem.title: The Problem
problem.intro: Coordinators built the daily schedule for clinicians visiting patients at home by hand:
items: Building the schedule took them 4 to 5 hours a day.
Visits ran late, and every delay meant a patient waiting at home.

An optimizer existed for driver-based patient transfers, but it didn't fit as is: there's no destination facility (the patient is the destination), no vehicle capacity (there's specialty), and appointments are already booked in the system.

insight.title: The mental model: review and adjust, not trigger
insight.body: Optimization runs on its own whenever an appointment is created or moved, so the coordinator opens a day that's already planned. The screen doesn't trigger anything: it's for reviewing and adjusting. The system never proposes changes by itself or reshuffles the schedule while someone is working. The optimized schedule is the baseline, and changes always belong to the coordinator.

flow.title: How the coordinator works
flow.desc: Automation with the person in control, end to end.

steps.text: Keeps the next 7 days optimized. Beyond that window it shows the raw schedule, marked as "not optimized".
Reviews the day as a Gantt, routes, map or list, with specialty as the main cut.
Adjusts what's needed: reassigns an appointment, pins it so it won't move, or sends it to "pending".
Compares before and after (kilometers and appointments) or tries another optimization criterion without touching the global settings.
Confirms, and only then are clinicians and patients notified in bulk. Or discards.
Sees in each appointment's list and detail what the system moved, with a "moved from X to Y".

gallery.title: Prototype screens
gallery.desc: Screenshots and recordings of the working prototype with fictional data. The same baseline handed off to engineering (UI in Spanish).

items.caption: Trying another criterion: the plan applies as a test, shows how much the day changed, and is discarded without touching the system schedule.
Routes view: visits, distance and driving time per clinician.

decisions.title: Key decisions
decisions.desc: Each decision balances efficiency with trust: an optimizer nobody understands is one nobody uses.

items.title: Continuity of care before efficiency
items.body: The patient keeps their usual clinician unless reassigning saves 20 or more minutes of travel. The trade-off is explicit and measurable.

items.title: Before / After always at hand
items.body: A toggle between the optimized route and the adjusted route, with kilometers and appointments, makes the cost of each adjustment visible.

items.title: Try without breaking
items.body: Coordinators can compare plans under other criteria (least travel, balanced load, most appointments) as a reversible trial.

items.title: Lock the day
items.body: A confirmed day doesn't re-optimize on its own. New appointments wait in "pending" until the coordinator chooses to add them.

items.title: Transparency for everyone else
items.body: Anyone who wasn't on the screen understands what the system changed: each moved appointment is flagged with where it moved from and to.

items.title: Real-operation states
items.body: The day in progress (past appointments aren't editable), missed visits with rescheduling, and optimizer errors with retry.

pivots.title: Course corrections
pivots.desc: What we changed after reviewing the prototype with product and with coordinators.

items.before: Pin appointments, then press "Re-optimize with my pins" in a separate bar
items.after: Pinning or unpinning re-optimizes the day instantly
items.why: One step and one concept fewer: pinning became just another adjustment, counted in the change summary.

items.before: Date, Before/After toggle, metrics and "Try" spread across separate rows, with the toggle inside the map
items.after: A single context bar with date, day range, Before/After, metrics and trial
items.why: Fewer places to look, and the same control behaves the same in the schedule and on the map.

results.title: Results
results.desc: Based on a comparison of the 3 months after launching in production.
items: Delays in home care went down.
The optimizer plans schedules a week ahead, and coordinators only make small adjustments when needed.
Coordinators trust the system to build schedules and spend the time they got back on other work.

items.title: Adopting automation depends on trust.
items.body: A schedule that doesn't move on its own and visible changes mattered as much as the algorithm's quality.

items.title: Human trade-offs have to be written down.
items.body: "Keep the clinician unless it saves 20 minutes" is a rule a team can debate. "Optimize" on its own isn't.

items.title: Reusing means reframing.
items.body: The transfer optimizer was a starting point, but it only worked once we redefined what a destination, a capacity and an appointment were.

summary.problem: Coordinators built the daily home-visit schedule by hand: 4–5 hours a day, with delays that left patients waiting.
summary.solution: An optimizer that keeps the week scheduled while the coordinator reviews, adjusts and confirms, with no surprise changes.
summary.impact: +32% medical visits in the 3 months after launch, 4–5 h saved per day and fewer delays.

design_system.title: A design system that lives in code
design_system.subtitle: Two shared libraries, one for web and one for mobile, used by 8 product frontends. Every decision is recorded in one place.
design_system.role_val: Product Designer: token definition, migration lead and close work with engineering

summary.problem: Each frontend built its own UI: three different mobile libraries, hard-coded colors and a Figma file that no longer matched production.
summary.solution: Two shared libraries, one per platform, built on semantic tokens and governed through PRs, ADRs and versioned releases.
summary.impact: 8 frontends use the same source of truth, dark mode comes from the tokens, and the MUI 7 migration shipped without breaking screens.

highlights.label: Frontends using the libraries (5 web, 3 mobile)
MUI 7 migration, validated screen by screen

cover.alt: Component library: Button documentation showing its contained, outlined, ghost and icon variants

problem.title: The Problem
problem.intro: The product is split into micro-frontends: about 5 in the web backoffice and 3 mobile apps. Each one built its own UI:
items: Each of the 3 apps had its own component library, so the same button, input or card existed in several versions.
Colors were hard-coded in every component, and states (hover, error, disabled) didn't match across screens.
Figma was the reference, but what shipped kept drifting from the design, and nobody could say which version of a component was the right one.

insight.title: Unify what you can, separate what you can't
insight.body: Web and mobile can't share a component library: MUI only exists for web, and mobile is better served by its own library with full control over behavior. So a single library wasn't forced. Everything that shares a platform was unified (the 3 apps moved to one library), and across platforms the tokens and criteria were shared instead of the code.

snippet.title: Tokens that say what a color is for, not what it looks like
snippet.desc: Three levels: primitives (the palette), semantic tokens (the role) and components. A component never knows a color value, only its role.
snippet.before_label: Before: the component knows the color
snippet.after_label: After: the component knows the role
snippet.note: Semantic tokens are grouped into bg, text, border, action and feedback. Each has a light and a dark value, so dark mode shipped without touching a single component.

flow.title: Migrating without breaking: a guided review
flow.desc: Moving to MUI 7 and applying the new styles affected every screen in 5 frontends. Manual review was unavoidable; AI agents made it targeted.

steps.text: Finds where each component is used across every screen: an impact map of the migration.
Turns that map into a guide of what to review and test, so nobody walks through screens blind.
Generates a visual before/after comparison of each screen as a reference.
Review screen by screen with regression and manual tests, guided by the map and the comparison.
Adopts the new library version only once its screens are validated.

gallery.title: The documentation is the product
gallery.desc: Each environment has a browsable component library with usage guidelines, props, states and examples. There's no design file to go stale: what's documented is what runs.

items.caption: Button usage guide: when to use it and when not to, with its import path and status.

decisions.title: Governance: every decision in one place
decisions.desc: What makes a design system last isn't the number of components, but how each change is decided and released.

items.title: Changes through PRs
items.body: Every new component or token goes through review. No single frontend changes everyone's library.

items.title: Decisions through ADRs
items.body: The big decisions (semantic tokens, MUI 7, a custom mobile library) are written down with their context and alternatives.

items.title: Versioned releases
items.body: A release skill builds each version and publishes it as a git tag, with notes organized into Added, Changed and Fixed.

items.title: Controlled adoption
items.body: Each frontend pins a tag in its package.json. A new version changes nothing until the team adopts it in its own PR.

pivots.title: Before and after
pivots.desc: The deeper changes the system left behind.

items.before: Three mobile libraries, one per app, with duplicated components
items.after: A single mobile library shared by the 3 apps
items.why: A component is designed, fixed and improved once.

items.after: Semantic tokens with light and dark values
items.why: Dark mode came from the tokens, and a rebrand would come down to changing the primitives.

items.before: Figma as the reference, drifting from production
items.after: Code as the only source: Figma was used to migrate and then deprecated
items.why: The design and what users see became the same thing.

results.title: Results
results.desc: What changed in the way the product is built.
items: Two shared libraries used by 8 frontends: 5 in the web backoffice and 3 mobile apps.
A single source of truth: updates happen in code and are traced through PRs and ADRs.
Dark mode solved with tokens, without touching components.
MUI 7 migration in 3–4 weeks, validated with QA through regression and manual tests, without breaking screens.
Discovery Hub prototypes use these same components, so the handoff needs no translation.

items.title: A design system lasts because of its governance, not its components.
items.body: PRs, ADRs and versioned releases made every change visible and reversible for every team.

items.title: Across platforms, share criteria, not code.
items.body: Forcing one library for web and mobile would have looked neater in a diagram and worked worse in practice.

items.title: AI doesn't replace review: it directs it.
items.body: The impact map and the before/after comparison didn't remove the need to check every screen, but they made that review targeted instead of blind.
